name: Battle of Caporetto
info: Austro-Hungarian forces reinforced by German units broke through the Italian line near Kobarid on the Isonzo front in October 1917, routed the Italian Second Army and drove the Italian army back to the Piave river.

facts.place: Near the town of Kobarid (Caporetto, Karfreit) and the river Isonzo, then in the Austrian Littoral, now in north-western Slovenia; the Italians then fell back about 150 kilometres to the Piave
facts.sides: The Kingdom of Italy, under Luigi Cadorna, with the Second Army commanded by Luigi Capello, against the Central Powers: Austro-Hungarian Army Group Boroević under Svetozar Boroević and a new 14th Army under the German Otto von Below, made up of nine Austrian and six to eight German divisions. The Italian army's effective strength was 1,800,000 before the battle.
facts.outcome: The Italian Second Army collapsed and the Italian army retreated to the Piave, its effective strength falling to 1,000,000; Cadorna was forced to resign and the government of Paolo Boselli fell.

t: The attack opened with gas fired from 894 tubes dug into a reverse slope, followed by a bombardment from 2,200 guns and an advance by specially trained stormtrooper units, which broke the Italian line between the IV and XXVII Corps.
Italian losses were 13,000 killed, 30,000 wounded and 265,000 to 275,000 prisoners, against about 70,000 casualties for the Austro-Hungarians and Germans.

The Central Powers' supply lines were stretched to breaking point and the advance stopped at the Piave, where the Italians held, and Italy went on to defeat the Austro-Hungarian army at Vittorio Veneto in 1918.
dyk: In Italian the name Caporetto came to stand for any terrible defeat: Mussolini called the failed general strike of 1922 the "Caporetto of Italian Socialism".
ev: The Italians launch numerous offensives on the Isonzo, the eleventh battle being the most successful in pushing back the Austro-Hungarians
Hindenburg and Arz von Straußenburg decide to send troops from the Eastern Front to the Isonzo, over Ludendorff's opposition
German experts led by the chemist Otto Hahn choose the quiet Caporetto sector for a gas attack
On the 24th the gas attack, the bombardment and the infantry assault break through the Italian line near Kobarid
Cadorna orders the retreat to the Tagliamento on the 30th
The Austro-Hungarians establish a bridgehead over the Tagliamento on the 2nd, and by the 10th Cadorna holds a line on the Piave and Monte Grappa
The British, French and Italian leaders meet at Rapallo from the 5th to the 7th
The Italians defeat the Austro-Hungarian army at Vittorio Veneto, and an armistice is signed on 3 November

sections.background:
Throughout the spring and summer of 1917 the Italians launched numerous offensives against the Austro-Hungarian lines on the Isonzo, the eleventh battle being the most successful in pushing the Austro-Hungarians back. Emperor Karl knew that a breakthrough could come at any moment, since both armies were exhausted and running out of men. He therefore wrote to Kaiser Wilhelm II and asked that German forces be sent to Italy.

In August 1917 Paul von Hindenburg and Arthur Arz von Straußenburg decided to send troops from the Eastern Front to the Isonzo. Erich Ludendorff was opposed but was overruled. In September three experts from the Imperial General Staff, led by the chemist Otto Hahn, went to the Isonzo front to find a site suitable for a gas attack. They proposed the quiet Caporetto sector, where a good road ran west through a mountain valley to the Venetian Plain. The Germans also sent Lieutenant General Konrad Krafft von Dellmensingen, an expert in mountain warfare, to reconnoitre the ground.

Lieutenant Colonel Georg Wetzell, Ludendorff's strategic adviser, advised him to use the German divisions to attack a weak point in the Italian line. The Italians inadvertently helped by providing weather information over their radio. Their air reconnaissance did notice the build-up of German and Austro-Hungarian forces in the region.
sections.forces:
The Central Powers deployed the Austro-Hungarian Army Group Boroević, commanded by Svetozar Boroević, which was prepared for the offensive. In addition a new 14th Army was formed with nine Austrian and six to eight German divisions, commanded by the German Otto von Below. The German divisions were Ludendorff's general reserve. Against them stood the Italian Second Army, whose commander Luigi Capello later fell ill with fever, under the supreme command of Luigi Cadorna. The Italian army as a whole had an effective strength of 1,800,000 troops.

The plan was for von Below's German divisions, guided by Konrad Krafft, to attack a part of the Julian Alps near the north-eastern corner of the Venetian salient. Meanwhile Boroević's Austro-Hungarian army would attack the eastern end of the salient and a stretch of ground near the Adriatic shore. Foul weather, a lack of readiness in some Austro-Hungarian divisions and in particular in their artillery delayed the attack by two days.

The attackers had 894 metal tubes, similar to Livens Projectors, dug into a reverse slope to fire gas canisters, and 2,200 guns. Specially trained and equipped stormtrooper units were to lead the assault with the new German model 08/15 Maxim light machine gun, light trench mortars, mountain guns, flamethrowers and hand grenades. Alpine troops were to protect the flanks by infiltrating the strong points and batteries on the ridges.
sections.course:
On 24 October there was no wind and the front was misted over. At 02:00 near Bovec (Plezzo) the 894 tubes were fired electrically at once, each canister holding 600 ml of a chlorine-arsenic agent and diphosgene, and smothered the Italian trenches in a dense cloud of poison gas. The defenders knew their gas masks would protect them for two hours or less and fled, but 500 to 600 were killed. At 06:41, 2,200 guns opened fire, many aimed at the valley road along which reserves were advancing. At 08:00 two large mines were detonated under strong points on the heights bordering the valley and the infantry attacked.

The infantry soon penetrated the almost undefended Italian fortifications in the valley, breaching the Second Army's line between the IV and XXVII Corps. Alpine troops took the strong points along the crests of Matajur and Kolovrat, laying telephone lines to keep in contact with their artillery. The attackers in the valley marched almost unopposed along the road, and some advanced 25 kilometres on the first day. Moving forces along the Italian front to stem the breakout only weakened other points and invited further attacks.

Capello, bedridden with fever, asked to withdraw to the Tagliamento, but Cadorna, who believed the force could regroup and hold out, refused. On 30 October Cadorna ordered most of the force to retreat across the Tagliamento, which took four days, with the Central Powers on their heels. On 2 November the 55th Infantry Division established a bridgehead across the river, but the Central Powers' supply lines were stretched to breaking point. By 10 November Cadorna held a position on the Piave and Monte Grappa.
sections.aftermath:
Italian losses were 13,000 killed, 30,000 wounded and 265,000 to 275,000 taken prisoner. Morale was so low among the Italian troops, mainly because of Cadorna's harsh disciplinary regime, that most of these surrendered willingly. The Italians also lost 3,152 artillery pieces, 3,000 machine guns and 1,712 mortars, along with a vast amount of stores and equipment. The Austro-Hungarians and Germans sustained around 70,000 casualties. The Italian army's effective strength fell from 1,800,000 to 1,000,000 and the government of Paolo Boselli collapsed.

Cadorna was forced to resign. Vittorio Emanuele Orlando, the Prime Minister, called the defeat a final straw. By the start of the battle Cadorna had sacked 217 generals, 255 colonels and 355 battalion commanders, and his troops detested him. He had directed the battle from some 30 kilometres behind the front and then retreated another 160 kilometres to Padua. Armando Diaz and Pietro Badoglio replaced him. Italian propaganda offices were set up, promising land and social justice to soldiers, and Italy accepted a more cautious strategy.

British, French and Italian leaders met at Rapallo from 5 to 7 November. Six French and five British infantry divisions were sent to Italy but played no part in the battle. The last push of the Austro-Hungarian and German forces, from 15 November to 23 December, was repelled at the First Battle of Monte Grappa, which secured the Italian positions south of the Piave.
sections.sources:
The battle is known in operational detail from Cyril Falls's one-volume history, The Battle of Caporetto, and from Erwin Rommel's interwar memoir and handbook Infanterie greift an, which describes the actions of Rommel and the units he led as a lieutenant. A commission set up by the Italian military in 1919 investigated the causes of the collapse. Of the Italian commanders, Badoglio, whose corps was easily overwhelmed in the early stages, escaped all charges during its hearings.

Historians differ in their emphasis. Brian R. Sullivan called Caporetto the greatest defeat in Italian military history, and John R. Schindler called it an unprecedented catastrophe for Italian arms. The disaster triggered a search for scapegoats, among them Cadorna. The use of stormtroopers and infiltration tactics developed in part by Oskar von Hutier is held to be demonstrated by the battle, and the poison gas used by the Germans is said to have had a large part in the collapse of the Italian Second Army.
sections.legacy:
The defeat led to the setting up in December 1917 of the Opera Nazionale Combattenti, an Italian charitable organisation that assisted veterans of the First World War and was closed in 1977. Lloyd George saw Caporetto as the latest episode in a year of confusion and cross-purposes in Allied strategy, and used the conference at Rapallo to gain approval of a Supreme War Council to improve military co-operation and develop a common strategy.

The Piave line later served as the springboard for the final Italian offensive, the Battle of Vittorio Veneto, on the anniversary of Caporetto, in which the Austro-Hungarian army was defeated after eleven days and an armistice was signed on 3 November 1918.

In Italy the word Caporetto came to denote a terrible defeat. Mussolini called the failed general strike of 1922 the "Caporetto of Italian Socialism", and for many years after the war the name was used to destroy the credibility of the liberal state. The battle appears in Ernest Hemingway's A Farewell to Arms, in Alessandro Baricco's Questa storia and in Christian Braw's novel Caporetto. Curzio Malaparte's La rivolta dei santi maledetti, published in 1921, was censored and suppressed and finally published in 1980. A museum in Kobarid is dedicated to the Isonzo battles and to Caporetto in particular.

summary: At Caporetto in October 1917 Austro-Hungarian and German forces used gas, a heavy bombardment and stormtroopers to break the Italian Second Army and drive the Italian army back to the Piave. Italian losses included 265,000 to 275,000 prisoners, and Cadorna was forced to resign.

M. Morselli, Caporetto 1917: Victory or Defeat? (Frank Cass, 2001)
John R. Schindler, Isonzo: The Forgotten Sacrifice of the Great War (Greenwood, 2001)
John Gooch, The Italian Army and the First World War (Cambridge University Press, 2014)
George H. Cassar, The Forgotten Front: The British Campaign in Italy 1917–18 (A&C Black, 1998)
notes: The article gives no strength for the Central Powers or for the Italian Second Army; only the Italian army's effective strength (1,800,000 before, 1,000,000 after) and the divisions of the 14th Army are given.
The article says the Italian effective strength 'declined from 1,800,000 to 1,000,000' in the lead; I attributed it to the army as a whole.
The article's sentence on the Battle of Pozzuolo and an encirclement during the Tagliamento crossing is unclear; I left it out.
The article says Badoglio commanded one of the corps overwhelmed; I wrote this without naming the corps.
Sources section: the article names no ancient-style accounts; it gives Falls, Rommel, the 1919 commission and later historians' verdicts only, so the section is short.
The article's phrase 'Cadorna was known to have maintained poor relations...' and the sacking figures are given as stated; they are not attributed to a named source in the article.
The ev entry for 1918 refers to the armistice of 3 November 1918; the article says the armistice was signed on 3 November after eleven days of fighting at Vittorio Veneto.
The article says 'the 55th Infantry Division (Austria-Hungary) established a bridgehead' after an attack by Captain Emil Redl's battalion; I omitted Redl.

Left out: Rommel's Pour le Mérite and his remarks on poorly fed troops; the Allied blockade and food shortages in Germany; the claim that Capello's withdrawal request and Cadorna's refusal are the cause of the later retreat.
